messages.body_plain:
Thanks Phil ! I was able to figure out the design matrices and successfully model interactions between items and person covariates. I had one more question - I was going through the examples that you provided with the mixedmirt() function. Specifically, this one:

#random slopes with fixed intercepts (suppressed correlation)
rmod3 <- mixedmirt(data, covdata, 1, fixed = ~ 0 + items, random = ~ -1 + pseudoIQ|group)
summary(rmod3)
(eff <- randef(rmod3))

eff$pseudoIQ contains 2 columns of 'pseudoIQ' and 'group'.

> eff$pseudoIQ
     pseudoIQ       group
G1 1.57032254 -0.05721247
G2 0.05408288  0.03605942
G3 1.08146330 -0.01116472

According to my understanding, this example is trying to include a random slope effect (random over the 3 groups) for pseudoIQ predictor in the model i.e., θ = β X + a*(pseudoIQ)+ ε, where a ~ N(0, \sigma). So, the 1st column in the output represents the 3 random slopes associated with the pseudoIQ predictor. I am not able to understand what the other column of 'group' contains. Does it mean that besides estimating random slope for pseudoIQ, it also estimates random intercepts of groups ? If that is the case, is there a way to suppress the calculation of random intercepts and just calculate the random slopes ? I tried to look at the matrix designs (using return.design = TRUE) to understand this but the 'Z' design matrix always turns out to be NaN. Can you please throw some light on this ?

Thanks,
Nishant

On Thursday, July 31, 2014 12:09:31 PM UTC-5, Phil Chalmers wrote:
>
> On Thu, Jul 31, 2014 at 11:04 AM, Nishant Verma <nisha...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Phil,
> >
> > Thanks for your reply. Yes, you are correct that if there are person-level covariates that affect the underlying latent traits (θ), then all items should illustrate the effects of these covariate terms. However, I was trying to point towards a slightly different scenario wherein, the covariate terms actually affect the item characteristic curves of certain items rather than the latent traits. I am not sure if statistical modeling theory has been developed for such scenarios. As an example, let us consider a test designed for measuring memory recall in subjects. Now, certain items on the test turn out to be biased because subjects belonging to a particular occupation are exposed to similar contents (as in the biased items) in everyday life and, therefore, they illustrate much higher likelihood of responding to those items correctly. During IRT modeling, this effect can be easily detected using DIF and, traditionally, such items may be removed from the test. If item deletion is not an option (such as in the case of retrospective analysis of tests that were not analyzed with IRT during design), separate IRT modeling of subject groups can also be performed. However, this would result in different item and subject scales. Therefore, it would be quite meaningful to have a methodology to be able to incorporate DIF effects within the model so that all subjects are measured on the same scale. For example, if DIF is uniform in nature, then the item response function (IRF) can contain a fixed intercept effect to adjust the difficulty parameter for certain subject groups.
>
> But this is exactly what an interaction of group membership by item does, create an extra intercept that only affects one group and not the other by design. So in short, yes this is possible to do in mixedmirt(), just specify a design matrix for items which you believe are systematically easier/more difficult given the group membership, and form an interaction term between the two in the model formula. Actually, if your model is a Rasch type this could also be done with lme4, so it might be good to check out the literature on how to do this with generalized mixed effects models as well (at least conceptually it will help).
>
> > In mathematical terms, this model will look as containing person-covariate terms in IRFs of only some items in the test. Such covariate terms will basically account for changes in IRF functions due to DIF across subject groups. However, if there are person-level covariate terms across all items in the test, that will account for factors that may affect the underlying latent traits - thereby, affecting all items in the test. Does this make any sense ?
>
> Yes it does, and it really does sound like a simple uniform DIF test for each item of interest (or modeled all at once). The key is to form the appropriate itemdesign data.frame and have the specific terms interact with the group membership. You'll need a column for each item of interest in the data.frame, but otherwise it should be easy to construct. Cheers.
>
> Phil

messages.body_plain:
Random slopes are always within the defined groups given by the | operator. This is true of other packages like nlme and lme4 since in order to define random variation of slopes the grouping factor has to be defined as well as the group intercept variation (the second column). So if you did something like this in lme4 with the syntax

dv ~ 0 _+ (cov | group)

and predicted the random effects with randef() you would get both a slope and intercept within the levels defined by group. The first example in the lme4::lmer() function shows the same effect. Cheers.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mehmet,

The output you are seeing is correct since the c parameters are always in reference to the first item (automatically fixed to 0 for identification). So negative values mean that the item 'is more difficult', or participants are more likely to endorse lower responses, compared to item 1. Positive values mean the opposite. It's really just an identification constraint and shouldn't change the interpretation of your rating scale model. Hope that helps.

Phil

On Thu, Aug 7, 2014 at 3:55 PM, Mehmet Gültaş <mehmet...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Phil,
>
> In terms of c parameter it makes perfect sense.
> Not in all of them but, in one of my specific grsm model fit trials (the one below) "a" parameters and also "d1,d2,d3,..." parameters are also chancing.
> Is it also normal. How should I interpret this difference?

The change in d's is almost always to be expected but is nothing to worry about. The d's are essentially configured around the first item since if you were to fit a standard graded/ordinal response model you should get intercept in the first item equal to those in the rating scale fixed intercepts (since (d1 + 0, d2 + 0, d3 + 0 )..... == (d1, d2, d3), so the d's in the rating scale are essentially the intercepts for the first item).

The a's on the other hand theoretically shouldn't change, but may be different since the tolerance criteria for the EM is rather weak (only .0001 since its so slow to converge). Perhaps fit both models with a more stringent criteria, and trying from random starting locations (with GenRandomPars = TRUE) to see if its a local minimum issue as well (doubtful, but you never know).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alexander,

Possible, yes, and it's something I played around with when I first added the EH method. Practical? Far from it. You'll notice that when the EH approach is run the number of quadrature nodes is set to 199 and the convergence tolerance dropped to 3e-5. These are to a) adequately capture the shape of the distribution during estimation and b) account for the added uncertainty in approximating the latent distribution at the same time as the item parameters.

The increase in quadrature make multidimensional models very unlikely at this point. Since they grow exponentially a 2-dimensional model would contain 199^2 = 39601 nodes to obtain the same degree of accuracy....which is obscene. A more reasonable number might be around 60 or less since that's only 3600, but from my experience with under 100 nodes it's hard to get an idea of what the real shape looks like (the distribution is extremely blocky). This is why the method is currently limited to unidimensional models. It should be possible to use an empirical histogram in the bifactor model for the primary dimension though, but I haven't added that yet. Cheers.

Phil

summary(group1mod, rotate = 'oblimin')
group2mod <- mod@pars[[2L]]
class(group2mod) <- 'ExploratoryClass'
summary(group2mod, rotate = 'oblimin')

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jan,

Using the above definitions, pass the objects to mirt.model(), where

model <- mirt.model(Q, COV=cov.factors)

and further send this on to mirt(). Unfortunately, on the current versions the variance terms are not freely estimated this way (only the covariances), but on the dev version variances are now detected. Either way, freeing variance terms is generally risky buisness since the models will become unidentified quickly, so I'd recommend leaving them as fixed at 1 for now.

Also, this isn't strictly a bifactor model (see ?bfactor for details), so you won't be able to capitalize on dimension reduction techniques for working with a larger number of latent variables. Given 5 factors, your best bet is probably the MHRM algorithm. Hope that helps.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Try the following code, and see the plot-method help file in mirt for other options. The last line plots the first 3 items all on the same plot.

```
library(mirt)
dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)
mod <- mirt(dat, 1)
plot(mod, type = 'trace')
plot(mod, type = 'trace', which.items = 1:3, facet_items=FALSE)
```

This also brings up another interesting point that many aren't aware of when making custom graphics. One of the main reasons I opted for the lattice package instead of using base R graphics (which looks to be the image attached here) was that the data is actually silently returned in the package whenever a plot is drawn. So, if you don't like the defaults, you can always extract the data and actually build your own, potentially with an entirely different plotting system. For example,

```
plt <- plot(mod, type = 'trace', facet_items=FALSE) #store the object
print(plt) #plot the object
str(plt) #find the data
plt$panel.args
pltdata <- data.frame(lapply(plt$panel.args, function(x) do.call(cbind, x))[[1]])
pltdata$item <- rep(colnames(dat), each = 50)
head(pltdata)

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(pltdata, aes(x, y, colour=item)) + geom_line() + ggtitle('ggplot2 Tracelines') +
    xlab(expression(theta)) + ylab(expression(P(theta)))
```

Phil

Hi Michael,

You definitely want to use the bfactor() function instead of mirt() here. mirt() uses a grid of quadrature for integration, and with the five factors defined here the quadpts are set equal to 3 (very bad and quite inaccurate). bfactor() uses a dimensional reduction algorithm to more accurately estimate the model, and in your case you'll want to build a two-tier model. This will also improve the accuracy of the M2 statistic (since dimensional reduction methods will be used there as well).

Onto the second part, beyond 2 dimensions (or 3 if slices are made at each level of the third factor....which I think may be supported in the plot generic) graphics can not be drawn since they are hyper-dimensional. itemplot() can work if you pass a drop.zeros = TRUE option, but for the full test information a plot is not possible. Cheers.

Phil

I find it to be much more of a blessing than a curse. The so-called "established" fit statistic cutoffs (which were all exclusively established for continuous variable models by the way....so the results you obtain from the WLSMV estimator in lavaan for categorical data likely are not what you think) are far too cookie-cutter for real data analysis. Fit measures are just tools to help understand different aspects of estimated models, and don't somehow represent a type of verisimilitude with the empirical world. I think every article proposing fit measures in SEM have emphasized this, so if anything regarding IRT fit measures we hopefully can learn not fall into the same pattern of mistakes that were made in SEM. At least, I certainly hope fit in IRT doesn't go down that path; time will tell.....Cheers.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
For model selection information statistics are still good candidates for the job, and the fit indices given in M2() are fine to use just so long as they don't carry the popular SEM definitions. E.g., a value of CFI = .85 shouldn't automatically be interpreted as an 'okay' fit, but rather that could be quite good for a categorical model, and may be an improvement over other competing models that were tested in this and other datasets. Interpret these stats for what they mean (i.e., the CFI measures how much worse a model fits, in terms of the chi-squared value, when only the intercept parameters are modeled relative to the parameters that were fit to the data....that could be useful to know, but then again it also seems rather ambiguous when you actually say it out loud).

If I had to place bets, I would probably say that the SRMR statistic and the associated residuals (as well as other item fit statistics) are more important than any global stat since they have very clear meanings globally and locally. That's not to say that they are the best, just that they are easier to interpret and fairly helpful with item analysis. IMO, it's much more important to know if particular areas of the model are functioning well rather than if the model globally fits the data exactly (which is a very difficult, and in many way a trially impossible task since statistical models are only approximations to the world anyway). Cheers.

Phil
